payload.text:
Observed 2026-08-16 during a supervised pass on basicly-e2mz.

The pass landed basicly-e2mz.13 and dispatched the curator at SHIP at 16:41. The log's last write was 16:41. Eleven minutes later the pass looked dead from outside. It was not.

Evidence taken at 16:48: the supervisor pid was alive since 16:19; the curator pid was state S with 19 threads; rchar moved 10.96 GB to 13.32 GB over 25 seconds; a tool subprocess was spawned mid-sample.

Why it matters: every lane dispatch prints a running line with elapsed seconds and a token count. A ship dispatch prints nothing. The architecture document also records that the ship dispatch carries no watchdog and no stream meter, so a wedged curator hangs the pass until the caller's own outer timeout, and an operator cannot tell that apart from normal work.

Adjacent to basicly-8veb but not the same defect. 8veb was the supervisor hiding progress when stdout is a pipe; lane progress reached the redirected file here without trouble.

Acceptance criteria. Given a supervised pass that dispatches a role at ship, when that dispatch is in flight, then the pass shall print a progress line carrying the role, the elapsed seconds and the token count, on the same cadence as a lane dispatch. Given that dispatch exceeds its bound, then a watchdog shall terminate it and record the reason rather than leaving the pass to the caller's outer timeout.

payload.description:
## Context

Found 2026-08-14, minutes after `basicly-zdtx` wired `health_coverage` onto the supervisor pass
line. The first thing the newly-wired report printed was a regression flag, and chasing it found a
defect in the report rather than in the runner.

```text
drift:  REGRESSED claude: fail 80% over the recent 5 vs 16% over 158 baseline runs (+0.64)
```

The recent five, ordered by timestamp through `health._agent_entries` — the reader's own path, not a
re-implementation:

```text
2026-08-13T09:23:19  executed
2026-08-13T09:26:15.529625  failed
2026-08-13T09:26:15.553781  failed
2026-08-13T09:26:15.556898  failed
2026-08-13T09:26:15.625860  failed
```

Four failures inside 96 milliseconds is not four lane failures. It is one event. The records name it:
`basicly-ca42`, `basicly-ef7t`, `basicly-efw2` and `basicly-rrah`, each `phase: lane`, each after
about 2,256 seconds of real work, and each carrying `stopped_bound: spend`. The session grant was
exhausted and the ceiling stopped every live lane at the same instant.

## The defect

`health` counts `outcome == failed` without reading `stopped_bound`, so a lane our own spend ceiling
halted is scored as an agent that failed. Over the whole ledger:

```text
claude failures                 29
  of which stopped_bound=spend   9   our budget stopped the lane
  of which no bound             20   the dispatch actually failed
```

So the reported 18 percent failure rate is really 12.3 percent, and the flagged regression is
**entirely** the ceiling: the recent window holds one executed run and four grant halts.

That matters more now than it did yesterday. Yesterday the number lived behind a command nothing
invoked. Today it prints on the pass line an operator reads before every dispatch, and it says a
runner is degrading when the ledger says the budget ran out. A signal that fires on the wrong cause
is worse than one nobody reads, because somebody acts on it.

## Why this is the health report's bug and not the ceiling's

The ceiling behaved correctly. `factory-loop.md` section 15.7 keeps it as a control precisely
because it has recorded correct firings, and that count is now **9 rather than the 5 measured on
2026-08-08** — four of them the event above. Nothing here argues for changing the ceiling.

It is also the same population question `basicly-izpi` answered this morning one layer down:
`decompose.unsized_lane_tokens` and `spend_accuracy` both exclude `FAILED` from the corpus, because
a lane that never finished is not evidence of what a lane costs. `health` is the third reader of the
same field and the only one that does not separate the causes.

## Acceptance

- While a run record carries `stopped_bound`, when the health report scores that agent, then the run
  is excluded from the failure rate and counted under its bound instead.
- When an agent's report is printed, then the count stopped by a bound is stated beside the failure
  rate rather than folded into it, so neither number hides the other.
- When drift is computed, then the recent and baseline windows apply the same exclusion, and the
  minimum sample rule is checked after it — a window emptied by the exclusion must not flag.
- Given the four `stopped_bound` records of 2026-08-13, when the report runs, then claude is not
  flagged as regressed.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/health.py`
- `src/basicly/supervise.py`
- `tests/test_health.py`

## Demonstration

`uv run basicly health` prints a failure rate that excludes bounded stops and names them separately,
and a supervised pass line reports no regression for claude against the committed ledger. A
regression test seeds four bounded stops in one window and asserts no flag, with a control of four
unbounded failures that does flag.

## Headroom, measured at main 3207fc6

```text
src/basicly/health.py     2404 / cap 4000     headroom 1596
tests/test_health.py      2860 / cap 4000     headroom 1140
src/basicly/supervise.py  frozen              check before adding a line
```

payload.text:
Found 2026-08-16 while filing basicly-e2mz.29 and basicly-e2mz.31 through the seam.

The seam refused two update fields, each with a precise remedy in the message:

  br update --acceptance-criteria has no owned-ledger equivalent, so mirroring it would drop the field br just wrote; add it to br_argv.UPDATE_FIELD_FLAGS
  br update --description has no owned-ledger equivalent, so mirroring it would drop the field br just wrote; add it to br_argv.UPDATE_FIELD_FLAGS

Measured: br_argv.UPDATE_FIELD_FLAGS holds only --external-ref, --type and -t. A seam-routed filing can therefore set a title and nothing else.

This is the seam behaving correctly. It stopped rather than diverging the two stores, which is the stated invariant. The defect is the narrowness of the translator, not the refusal.

Consequence today: basicly-e2mz.29 and basicly-e2mz.31 carry their evidence and criteria as comments, and neither has a structured acceptance_criteria field, so the definition-of-ready lint will block both until this lands. That is why both declare a blocks dependency on this issue.

Acceptance criteria. Given a seam-routed br update that names a field the owned ledger can hold, when the write runs, then the seam shall translate and mirror it rather than refuse. Given a field the owned ledger genuinely cannot hold, then the refusal shall stand and shall name the field.

payload.title: correct the architecture claim that the curator is inert under the supervisor

payload.text:
Observed 2026-08-16 during a supervised pass on basicly-e2mz.

docs/architecture/architecture.md, section Roles at dispatch, states:

  The curator and the retrospector are both inert on the supervised landing pass, which has no watchdog and no stream meter of its own. Under the supervisor they run only after the ship approval, on the interactive driver.

The run contradicts the second sentence. After basicly-e2mz.13 landed, the curator was dispatched with the supervisor process itself as its parent, not an interactive driver. Preflight had reported 'ship pending - the live L3 grant delegates it', so the supervisor approved the ship itself and dispatched.

The first sentence appears to hold: the dispatch showed no progress line and no watchdog, which is basicly-e2mz.29.

Acceptance criteria. Given the architecture document is read at the Roles at dispatch section, when it describes where the curator runs under a supervised pass, then it shall state that the supervisor dispatches the curator itself once a grant delegates the ship approval, and it shall not claim an interactive driver is required.

Fresh observation that settles this bead, 2026-08-17 on basicly-vkh0.27, a single-lane loop run rather than a supervised pass.

The curator ran and produced its artifact. The unit's own ledger events, in order:

    comment  [harness-policy] checkpoint=ship approved under grant L3
    comment  [harness-cost] id=basicly-vkh0.27#cost
    comment  [harness-run] id=basicly-vkh0.27#run-3baf1603bf phase=ship
    status
    comment  [harness-run] id=basicly-vkh0.27#run-3baf1603bf-2 phase=ship
    comment  [harness-artifact] kind=release-record {"claims":[{"claim":"feat(tracker): read gate state from the owned fold ...

The release-record artifact is the curator's output, and two ship-phase run records carry its dispatches: 1780766 and 1793781 tokens. So the curator is reachable and does work on a landing.

What this does not establish: the claim being corrected is about the curator under the **supervisor**, and this observation is from `basicly loop run`, not `basicly loop supervise`. `loop._dispatch_curation` documents itself as skipped under the supervisor's landing pass, which has no watchdog or stream meter of its own. So the honest correction is narrower than "the curator runs": it runs on a direct advance and is deliberately skipped on a supervised landing, and the architecture text should say which.

Supporting population figure: of 202 cost records in the ledger, 194 report a dispatch count equal to their run-record count and 8 report fewer. Those 8 are the units that curated - which is also the measure of how rare a curated landing is.

The architecture edit is held: `docs/architecture/architecture.md` is inside the declared scope of the running basicly-vkh0.29 lane, and two writers on one file is how a clean merge drops a field.

Two findings, 2026-08-17, and together they say this bead is probably already satisfied.

First, the architecture text this bead names appears correct as it stands. It reads: "The curator and the retrospector are both inert on the supervised landing pass, which has no watchdog and no stream meter of its own. Under the supervisor they run only after the ship approval, on the interactive driver." That matches loop._dispatch_curation own docstring, which says it is skipped under the supervisor landing pass, and it matches an observation from today: on basicly-vkh0.27, driven by basicly loop run rather than by supervise, the curator ran and appended a release-record artifact with the claims bound to evidence, at 1780766 and 1793781 tokens across two ship-phase runs.

Second, this bead carries a title and nothing else. No description, no acceptance criteria, no design notes. So the claim it says is wrong is not written down anywhere, and a reader cannot tell whether the text was corrected already or whether a different sentence was meant. It is one of three open records in that state.

Recommendation: close it as already true, or replace the title with the exact sentence that is wrong and where it lives. Not closed here, because closing a bead on the strength of my reading of a document it does not quote is the same error the bead was filed about.

One thing that genuinely is unverified and is not this bead: no supervised pass has been observed running the curator after ship approval. The text asserts that path; the ledger has not recorded it.

## The defect

`docs/architecture/architecture.md` §30 *Roles at dispatch* carries this as the first of two
caveats:

> The curator and the retrospector are both inert on the supervised landing pass, which has
> no watchdog and no stream meter of its own. Under the supervisor they run only after the
> ship approval, on the interactive driver.

The first sentence holds. **The second does not.** Under the supervisor, both roles run on the
supervisor's own process after it approves the ship itself, and the driver the supervisor uses
to get there cannot switch them off even in principle - `loop.run_until_blocked` takes no
`repair_dispatch` parameter, so the ship advance runs with `advance`'s default of `True`.

So the text sends a reader looking for an interactive driver that is not in the picture, on
the one path where an unmetered dispatch actually happens.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Read the claim:

       rg -n -A3 'inert on the supervised landing pass' docs/architecture/architecture.md

2. Read the two dispatches the claim is about, and the flag that gates each:

       rg -n -A3 'def _dispatch_curation' src/basicly/loop.py
       rg -n 'if root is None or not ctx.repair_dispatch' src/basicly/loop.py

3. Read what the supervisor passes on each of its two advances:

       rg -n 'loop.advance\(|loop.run_until_blocked\(' src/basicly/supervise.py

4. Read whether the second of those can pass the flag at all:

       rg -n -A9 'def run_until_blocked' src/basicly/loop.py

5. Confirm which process approved the ship on a real supervised pass: read the pass log for
   the `ship pending - the live L3 grant delegates it` preflight line and then check the
   parent process of the curator's dispatch.

Observed, verified in code 2026-08-19 at main 9534ca05:

- `supervise._land_green` passes `repair_dispatch=False` to the build->verify
  `loop.advance` (`src/basicly/supervise.py:3971`), with a comment giving exactly the reason
  the architecture text gives. That is sentence one, and it is correct.
- Once `policy.approve_checkpoint_guarded(..., interactive=False, grant_root=session.root_issue)`
  approves - which an L3 grant does, with no human in it - the same function ships through
  `loop.run_until_blocked(repo_root, outcome.issue_id, grant_root=session.root_issue)`
  (`supervise.py:3998`). `supervise.advance_parked` reaches the same driver.
- `loop.run_until_blocked` has **no** `repair_dispatch` parameter and calls
  `advance(repo_root, issue_id, config=..., inputs=..., grant_root=...)`, so
  `repair_dispatch` takes its default `True`. `loop._dispatch_curation` and
  `loop._retrospective` are gated only on that flag, so both fire - in the supervisor
  process.
- The behavioural half was already observed 2026-08-16 on a supervised pass over
  `basicly-e2mz`: after `basicly-e2mz.13` landed, the curator was dispatched with the
  supervisor process itself as its parent, and preflight had reported
  `ship pending - the live L3 grant delegates it`.

Expected: §30 states that the supervisor dispatches the curator and the retrospector itself
once a grant delegates the ship approval, names the driver that does it, and does not claim an
interactive driver is required.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given `docs/architecture/architecture.md` §30 is read at the *Roles at dispatch* caveats
  when it describes where the curator and the retrospector run under a supervised pass, then
  it states that the supervisor dispatches them itself once a grant delegates the ship
  approval, and it does not claim an interactive driver is required.
- Given the corrected text then it distinguishes the build->verify landing, which passes
  `repair_dispatch=False`, from the ship advance, which cannot pass it - so a reader learns
  which of the supervisor's two advances is metered and which is not.
- Given the corrected text then every claim in it names the module and function a reader can
  check it against, rather than describing a driver.
- Demonstrated by: reading the edited section against
  `rg -n 'loop.advance\(|loop.run_until_blocked\(' src/basicly/supervise.py` and
  `rg -n -A9 'def run_until_blocked' src/basicly/loop.py`, with no sentence left that the
  two outputs contradict.

## Scope

- `docs/architecture/architecture.md`

payload.title: a second teardown of an already cleaned worktree fails the whole pass

payload.text:
Observed 2026-08-16 on a supervised pass over basicly-e2mz with --max-passes 3.

Both lanes landed and both worktrees were cleaned. The pass then attempted a SECOND teardown of one of them and exited 1. The final three lines of the run:

  Cleaned up worktree 'basicly-e2mz-16' (worktree + branch + metadata).
  no worktree named 'basicly-e2mz-16': no session record and no registered worktree matches it. Run `git worktree list` to see them.
  SUPERVISE EXIT 1

Two consequences, and the second is the expensive one.

1. The pass reports failure after a fully successful round. basicly-e2mz.13 merged as 8ccf6d5 and closed; basicly-e2mz.16 merged as ada298a with verify green.

2. basicly-e2mz.16 was left OPEN at phase ship with a worktree binding to basicly-e2mz-16, which no longer exists on disk. `basicly loop status basicly-e2mz.16` reports that binding against a `git worktree list` that does not hold it. An open bead whose work has landed is the exact trap recorded on basicly-u6jq.1: the next pass adopts it and provisions a worktree for work that already shipped.

The teardown is not idempotent, and it should be. A teardown of an already absent worktree states the same fact as a teardown that ran.

Acceptance criteria. Given a lane whose worktree has already been torn down, when teardown runs again, then it shall report the worktree as already absent and exit zero rather than raising. Given a lane that has merged and passed verify, when its teardown raises for any reason, then the pass shall still clear the lane's worktree binding and shall not leave the bead open at ship.

Observed 2026-08-17 on basicly-vkh0.27, one layer over from the teardown case this bead names. A redundant ship advance on a unit already at done exits non-zero with an upstream error rather than reporting that there is nothing to do:

  Error: br close basicly-vkh0.27 --reason shipped by the harness loop failed: Warning: Skipped basicly-vkh0.27: already closed
  Error: Nothing to do: all 1 issue(s) skipped

The unit had already shipped correctly in the previous advance. Nothing was lost. The cost is that an operator reading exit codes cannot tell a redundant advance from a failed one, which is the same failure mode as the second teardown.

Same remedy shape if this bead is widened: an advance whose work is already done reports it and exits zero.

The redundant advance is not free, which is worth adding to the argument for this bead.

The third advance on basicly-vkh0.27 described in the previous comment spent 1793781 tokens before it failed on the already-closed bead. Its run record is basicly-vkh0.27#run-3baf1603bf-2, phase=ship.

So a redundant advance re-dispatches an agent at about 1.8 million tokens and then exits non-zero with an upstream error. Reading it as a failure and retrying costs the same again. That moves this bead from a legibility complaint to a measured spend leak.

## Context

On 2026-08-16 every lane failure in the session was operator error, not an engine defect. The engine refused correctly and named the cause every time. The owner asked for a remedy, and the remedy is not simply more prose in the always-on files.

This repository already states the hierarchy: git hooks are the deterministic floor, and guidance is what you use when a gate cannot express the check. The always-on baseline is also measured at 7014 to 7343 characters and is at its cap, so a new always-on rule costs something real and must earn it.

## The four failures and the tier each one belongs in

1. A stray 7.6 MB file under the tracker directory was committed by the tracker-state rollup, which stages the whole directory. CODE. Filed as basicly-vkh0.31.
2. The ignore list missed the file because it is a denylist of suffixes and the name ended `.recovered` rather than `.db`. CODE, same bead: stage known paths instead of relying on ignore rules.
3. `basicly loop run` on a child defaults the session root to the child, so a grant on the parent is never consulted, and the refusal does not name the `--root` flag that fixes it. Two dispatch attempts died on this. CODE: either default a child root to its parent, or name the flag in the refusal text.
4. A subagent was told to write its output into `docs/architecture/` inside the base checkout. An actively written file in the base checkout blocks every lane landing, and it blocked three. GUIDANCE: no gate can see the intent behind a subagent brief.

## What this bead must not become

A fragment that says be careful. Each item above either becomes a check that refuses the thing, or it does not land. Item 4 is the only guidance candidate, and it should be authored as a catalog source, never a hand-written discoverable markdown file, per the catalog-authoring rule.

## Sequencing

Run after the architecture rewrite is verified and swapped in. The rewrite renumbers sections that code cites, and doing both at once would tangle two unrelated diffs.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given each of the four failures when its remedy has landed then three are deterministic checks that refuse the failing input and name the cause, and the fourth is a catalog-authored guidance entry scoped to the narrowest tier that reaches the reader
- Given a proposed remedy that is only prose advising more care then it is rejected and the bead records why

## Scope

- `src/basicly/merge.py`
- `src/basicly/cli.py`
- `.basicly/core/fragments/**`
- `tests/**`

## Second occurrence of the same defect, 2026-08-16

The session-root flag has now cost two separate stalls, hours apart, and the second was after the first was already understood and filed. That makes it a control problem, not an attention problem.

Occurrence 1. `basicly loop run <child>` defaults the session root to the child, so the grant on the parent is never consulted:

    [blocked] intake -> intake: classify needs an agent-proposed work type; no active grant
    on basicly-vkh0.26 to delegate it under

Two dispatch attempts died before the `--root` flag was read.

Occurrence 2. `basicly loop advance` has NO `--root` flag at all - only `loop run` does. Shipping three landed beads with `loop advance` therefore produced:

    [blocked] verify -> verify: ship checkpoint awaiting human approval

on all three, from an L3 grant that delegates ship, because the grant was looked for on the child.

## Why the refusal text is the fix

Both messages are accurate and neither is actionable. The first names the missing grant without naming the flag that supplies it. The second reports a human checkpoint without saying that a grant exists one level up and was not consulted.

Two candidate remedies, and the second is cheaper:

1. Default a child's session root to its parent when the child carries no grant of its own.
2. Name `--root` in both refusals when the issue has a parent that carries a live grant, and give `loop advance` the flag it lacks.

A reader who hits either message should not have to run `--help` to discover the mechanism that would unblock them.

## Bearing on the tier question this bead exists to settle

This is the clearest case yet for the bead's own rule. No fragment saying remember the root flag would have helped: I knew about the flag when occurrence 2 happened, and it still cost a dispatch, because `loop advance` does not accept it. Guidance cannot fix a missing flag.

payload.description:
## Steps to Reproduce

`FORCE_COLOR=3` is set in this machine shell environment. Measured 2026-08-16:

    uv run pytest tests/test_ui.py -q
    10 failed, 3 passed

    env -u FORCE_COLOR -u COLORTERM uv run pytest tests/test_ui.py -q
    13 passed

Observed: ANSI escapes such as `\x1b[32m` and `\x1b[2m` leak into output the tests assert as plain text.

Expected: the suite gives the same verdict whatever the ambient colour configuration.

## Why this is worse than one flaky file

A lane spawned from a shell carrying the variable inherits it, so its verify run fails on code that cannot affect colour. Two lanes burned rework on exactly that: `basicly-vkh0.28`, a kit CLI, and `basicly-e2mz.30`, the tracker seam.

**The whole suite passed while the single file failed.** A green `uv run pytest -q` therefore does not clear this, and the order dependence is itself the defect: some other test disables colour globally, and whichever runs first decides the verdict. That is a shared-state leak between tests.

## Do not fix this in the shell

The repository rule is that a fix lives in the repo. Stripping the variable at dispatch is a workaround for today, not the remedy. The suite must neutralise the ambient value itself, and a test must not depend on another test having done so.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given any value of FORCE_COLOR CLICOLOR_FORCE or NO_COLOR in the environment when the suite runs then every test gives the same verdict as it does with those variables unset
- Given tests/test_ui.py runs alone when the environment forces colour then it passes, without relying on any other test having run first

## Scope

- `tests/conftest.py`
- `tests/test_ui.py`

## Steps to Reproduce

Dispatch a lane whose diff adds an engine module or a test file. `basicly-vkh0.28` adds `.basicly/core/kit/tracker/cli.py` and `tests/test_kit_tracker_cli.py`; `basicly-e2mz.30` is the same shape.

At the landing:

    [escalated] build -> build: merge failed: verify full failed: pytest, docs-claims (rework 2/2)
    docs-claims: docs/plan/implementation-plan.md [plan-current-state]: generated block is stale
      run `uv run python .scripts/docs_claims.py --fix`

The pytest half is not a second cause: the failing tests are `tests/test_docs_claims.py` and `tests/test_docs_claims_consumer.py`, which assert the same check.

Measured 2026-08-16: the base checkout is clean before the merge (`docs_claims.py --check` prints 4 generated blocks current, 5 assertions current, exit 0). The block goes stale only in the merged tree, because `plan-current-state` counts engine modules and test files.

`basicly-vkh0.26` landed cleanly on the same base at the same time. The difference is that it modified existing files and added none.

## Why the lane cannot fix it

`docs/plan/implementation-plan.md` is outside every lane scope, and correctly so. A lane that widened into it would take a path other lanes also touch. So the lane is refused for a defect it is not permitted to repair, and it burns its whole rework budget discovering that.

## The engine already knows the file is regenerable

Preflight prints it:

    regen: generated: a landing conflict confined to these is rebuilt and continues, spending no rework
           `docs/plan/implementation-plan.md` <- `uv run python .scripts/docs_claims.py --fix --block plan-current-state`

That path covers a merge CONFLICT confined to those files. It does not cover a generated block going stale because the merge changed the tree the block is derived from. Those are the same class and only one is handled.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given a lane whose merge leaves a declared-regenerable file stale when the landing runs verify then the engine shall regenerate that file after the merge and before verify, and shall not charge the lane rework for it
- Given regeneration does not make the file current when the landing runs then the failure shall be reported against the file with the command that would fix it, rather than as a plain verify failure

## Scope

- `src/basicly/merge.py`
- `tests/test_merge.py`

## Steps to Reproduce

Measured 2026-08-16. `basicly-vkh0.32` was refused at the landing:

    [blocked] build -> build: basicly-vkh0.32 changed .importlinter, docs/plan/implementation-plan.md,
    src/basicly/br.py, src/basicly/edge_adoption.py, tests/test_edge_adoption.py,
    tests/test_tracker_cutover.py outside its declared scope
    (src/basicly/tracker_cutover.py, tests/test_tracker_adoption.py), and basicly-b2n2 declared
    that ground: the plan is wrong, not the merge.

Half of that refusal was correct and is not this bead: the scope declaration really was wrong, and the gate said so precisely.

The other half was a collision with a lane that had produced nothing:

    git log --oneline main..harness/basicly-b2n2 | wc -l    -> 0
    git -C <worktree> status --short | wc -l                -> 0

Zero commits ahead of main, clean worktree, sitting on a base from an earlier session. `basicly-b2n2` had held `src/basicly/br.py` and a worktree slot since before the session while writing no code.

Tearing the worktree down released the ground and the lane landed. Nothing was lost, because there was nothing to lose.

## The gap

The architecture defines live deliberately: "Live means the worktree session records on disk, not the tracker export." The reason is good and should not be reverted - a freshly provisioned lane is the one most likely to be mid-edit, and the export would not show it.

But presence of a worktree record is a weak proxy for occupancy. It cannot distinguish:

- a lane mid-edit with uncommitted work, which must hold its ground;
- a lane with commits, which must hold its ground;
- a lane with no commits and a clean tree, which is holding a claim and a concurrency slot and nothing else.

The third case cost a landing, a rework attempt, and an operator decision today. It also occupied one of five worktree slots, which separately blocked a dispatch earlier in the same session.

## What this is not

Not an argument for reading the tracker export instead. Not an argument for auto-reaping a lane: a human parked it for a reason, and deleting work is the one thing a scope gate must never do. A lane with no commits but a dirty tree is genuinely mid-edit and must keep its ground.

The remedy is discrimination and a better message, not eviction.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given a scope collision with a lane that has no commits ahead of the base and no uncommitted changes when the landing gate reports the collision then it names that lane as holding no work, and names the command that releases it
- Given a collision with a lane that has commits or uncommitted changes then the refusal is unchanged
- Given the preflight runs when a provisioned lane has no commits and a clean tree then it reports that lane as holding a slot without work

## Scope

- `src/basicly/merge.py`
- `src/basicly/contention.py`
- `tests/test_merge.py`

## Steps to Reproduce

A durability review of docs/architecture/architecture.md on 2026-08-16 found the systemic defect behind most of its individual ones. The document declares status out of scope at line 138 and then carries roughly twenty status paragraphs and four capability-status columns.

The two files had already diverged on one surface. Three gradings of the tool-call boundary existed at once:

    architecture.md  layer 1                     partial
    status.md        enforcement at the boundary designed
    status.md        agent hooks for two families shipped

Architecture defines `designed` as "decided, sequenced behind a later phase, and nothing is built". Four hooks exist and are projected, so `designed` was false while a `shipped` row described the same four hooks.

A second contradiction sat inside architecture alone: two gates were graded `partial` for behaviour a later section argues for as a deliberate design decision, in the section the grading links to.

## What was fixed immediately, and what was not

Fixed in the same session: both status columns deleted from the two gate tables, so only one file can be wrong about a grade. Also the four falsehoods the review found - the lens vocabulary never named, a module count that did not reproduce from its cited source, a census figure copied in defiance of the decision record that forbids copying it, and a dependency register omitting the dependency with its own decision record.

Not fixed, and the reason this issue exists: the pattern will recur. The review identifies roughly 420 lines that go stale when the CODE changes rather than when a DECISION changes, spread across many sections.

## The prerequisite the review names, which is the useful part

Most of the content that should leave architecture lands in `status.md`. `status.md` itself records that **nothing gates it**. Moving a stale row from a file nobody gates into another file nobody gates does not reduce the risk; it relocates it.

Architecture decision **D-30** proposes one source rendered into every surface by a generated block. It is recorded as `proposed`, not accepted, and not built. **D-30 is therefore a prerequisite of the cleanup, not an item beside it.** Decide D-30 first.

## Why this matters more than a tidy-up

An agent reads the architecture folder at the start of every session and builds its working context from it. A false statement there is not a documentation defect; it is a wrong premise under every unit of work that follows. That is the owner's framing and it is the right one.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given a capability with a status when the reader looks for it then exactly one file states that status, and the architecture document states only what the capability is and what it must satisfy
- Given the architecture document is read after a routine refactor that changes no decision then no sentence in it has become false
- Given D-30 is decided when the cleanup runs then the destination of every moved row is a surface something gates

## Scope

- `docs/architecture/architecture.md`
- `docs/architecture/status.md`
- `.scripts/docs_claims.py`

payload.description:
## Context

A quarter of the open backlog cannot be dispatched, and nothing says so until someone tries one bead at a time.

Measured 2026-08-17 over `.beads/issues.jsonl`, 221 open records:

| Population | Count |
| --- | --- |
| acceptance criteria in the structured field | 134 |
| field empty, but the description carries an `## Acceptance Criteria` heading | 32 |
| criteria nowhere at all | **55**, of which 52 are not epics |

The discriminator is proven rather than assumed, with one probe per population:

    basicly policy dor basicly-vkh0.36   ->  DoR: READY          (field populated)
    basicly policy dor basicly-e2mz.35   ->  DoR: READY          (heading in the description only)
    basicly policy dor basicly-y8el      ->  DoR: NOT READY - missing: ## Acceptance Criteria

So the heading in the description is sufficient and the field is not required. The 55 have neither, and every one of them stops at classify with the same refusal. 24 of them are priority 1.

The count is a floor rather than a ceiling: the readiness check answers more than the criteria question, so a record that passes this filter can still be refused for another missing section.

## Why it is worth a bead rather than an afternoon

Two reasons, and the second is the one that makes it a mechanism problem.

A dispatch on any of the 55 costs a worktree provisioning and an intake advance before the refusal, so the cost of the gap is paid per attempt rather than once.

And the readiness rules are not ours yet. `policy.definition_of_ready` spawns the external binary's `lint`, which is the first of the operations with no owned equivalent, and porting it is inside `basicly-wpc8.1`. Whoever owns those rules chooses whether the description heading keeps counting. That choice moves this number in either direction, so the report has to read the live rule rather than restate it.

## What to build

A report that names every open record the readiness check refuses, with the reason it gives, so the gap is one command rather than 221 probes. It reads the live check rather than re-implementing its rules.

Then the authoring pass itself, which is the improvement controller's kind of work: 52 small edits, each writing criteria for a record whose intent is already in its title and description.

## Contention to respect

Folding this into `basicly policy dor --all` would touch `src/basicly/policy.py` and `src/basicly/cli.py`. Both are inside the declared scope of open beads, `basicly-wpc8.1` and `basicly-wpc8`, so the report starts as a script instead. Adding a `[[verify.checks]]` entry touches `basicly.toml`, which `basicly-vkh0.29` declares and `basicly-vkh0.37` is amending, so sequence it after those rather than beside them.

## Scope

- `.scripts/report_readiness.py`
- `tests/test_report_readiness.py`

payload.value:
Given the open record set when the readiness report runs then it names every record the readiness check refuses and the reason each refusal gives
Given the readiness rules change then the report follows them, because it calls the live check rather than restating its rules
Given a record that passes the check then it does not appear in the report, proven against a record known to pass
Given the report after the authoring pass then no non-epic open record is refused for missing acceptance criteria
Demonstrated by: uv run python .scripts/report_readiness.py

Breakdown by what is missing: 24 missing Acceptance Criteria alone, 15 missing Steps to Reproduce alone, 11 missing Success Criteria alone, 8 missing both Steps to Reproduce and Acceptance Criteria, 1 missing both Success Criteria and Acceptance Criteria. Note Scope is absent from the missing list entirely, so every open record already declares one. TWO POPULATIONS, and only the second is authoring work. Twenty records were a one word heading error, ## Acceptance where the reader wants ## Acceptance Criteria, and those were renamed and reconciled to zero earlier today in 90aac8f0. The 59 above are the remainder and need real content. A WARNING ON INSTRUMENTS: my own regex over the folded description reported 87 records with no parseable scope and 9 with a malformed one. Both figures were wrong. The engine predicate disagreed, and the engine predicate is the one the gate uses. Use policy.definition_of_ready, never a description regex, and treat a dotfile such as .importlinter or .gitignore as a real path rather than junk.

payload.description:
## Context

A lane that hits the runner timeout tries a salvage commit. When that commit is rejected, the advance prints a **passing** hook line as the reason, so an operator reading the message goes to the wrong gate.

Observed 2026-08-17 on basicly-wpc8.1, verbatim:

    [blocked] classify -> classify: runner 'claude' stopped on runner_timeout after 3600s
    in worktree 'basicly-wpc8-1'; the salvage commit was rejected:
    protect-generated-commit.................................................Passed;
    inspect the worktree and re-dispatch

`protect-generated-commit` passed. So did every hook in that list. The actual cause was one stale citation, found by running the commit by hand and reading the whole output:

    docs/requirements/factory-loop.md: 1 stale citation(s); this document has no recorded debt
      - line 85: merge.py:509 - past end-of-file or a blank line

The lane had moved a function in `merge.py`, so a parenthetical line reference in another document landed on a blank line. A one-line fix, hidden behind a message naming a gate that was fine.

## The defect

The reporter appears to take the **last** line of the hook output rather than the failing one. A pre-commit run ends with its passing hooks after the failing one has already printed, so the last line is almost always a pass. The message is therefore not merely unhelpful, it is reliably wrong whenever more than one hook runs.

## Why it costs more than it looks

A timed-out lane is already the expensive case: the tokens are spent and the work is uncommitted. The operator's next decision is whether to salvage by hand or re-dispatch, and that decision needs the real cause. Pointing at a passing gate argues for re-dispatch, which pays the whole lane cost again to arrive at the same one-line fix.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/runner.py`
- `src/basicly/loop.py`
- `tests/test_loop.py`

Given no hook output can be attributed then the message says so rather than quoting an unrelated line
Demonstrated by: uv run pytest tests/test_loop.py -k salvage -q

payload.description:
## Context

Found by the `basicly-w88t` lane 2026-08-14 and verified by hand at main before filing. That lane
made the repair brief carry per-lens reviewer findings. It then reported that nothing dispatches
against the brief while the unit rests in `validate`, which makes the improvement unreachable on the
path it was built for.

Three observations, each read from the tree rather than reasoned:

```text
loop.py:374            the ONLY call to _repair_in_place, inside _on_build (starts 358)
loop.py:438            _on_validate calls _rework on a failed gate
loop.py:2114           _rework records an attempt and blocks, escalating at the cap
loop_state.py:191-192  ("ship", landed and not validating) precedes ("validate", landed and
                       validating), so a landed validating unit pins at validate
supervise.py:1577      ready_lanes takes _phase_of(...) == "build" only
```

So a failed `validate-as-consumer` spins on `_rework` to its cap and escalates to a human. No repair
is dispatched, and the brief the reviewer findings now populate waits in the worktree until the unit
is returned to build by hand. The composition itself works — the `w88t` lane demonstrated the brief
being consumed once the unit is at build — so this is a missing route, not a broken brief.

## Why the obvious fix is not obviously right

Two routes exist and each has a named hazard, which is why this is filed rather than taken.

Changing `derive_phase` so a failing validate falls back to `build` returns the unit to a phase whose
work is already merged into base. A repair commit then lands on a branch whose content is upstream,
which is the shape that lost committed work before `basicly-5vu4`.

Adding a re-land step to `_on_validate` keeps the phase and needs the same spend gate the validate
dispatch already carries. Note `basicly-xab3` landed the grant root into both supervised drives on

payload.description:
## Context

`loop run` refuses to advance when the base checkout has **any** uncommitted change, including changes in files the incoming merge cannot touch. So one piece of unrelated work in progress blocks every lane landing, and the operator's only remedies are to commit work that is not ready or to discard it.

Observed 2026-08-17. basicly-wpc8.1 was green in its worktree — 4295 passed — and committed at 89a5436. The build-to-verify advance, which is the only step that merges, refused:

    base checkout has uncommitted changes; commit or stash first:
    M .basicly/core/kit/tracker/differential.py
    M src/basicly/cost_rollup.py
    ... 13 more, none of them in the lane's commit

Not one of the dirty paths appears in the lane's commit, so `git merge` itself would not have refused. The precondition is broader than the operation it protects.

## Why the broad form was chosen, and why it is still worth narrowing

The broad check is safe and cheap, and it prevents a class of confusion where a landing silently mixes an operator's work into a lane's merge. That reason is real. What it does not distinguish is dirt that **could** conflict from dirt that provably cannot.

The narrowing is checkable rather than judged: the merge's own file set is known before it runs, and so is the dirty set. Refuse on the intersection, on the engine tracker paths the advance itself commits, and on anything the rebase would regenerate. Admit the rest, and say in the advance detail which dirt was admitted, so nothing is silent.

## The operating cost this has today

Parallel work in the base checkout serialises against lane landings. An operator running several agents in one checkout - which is the obvious way to keep a backlog moving while a lane runs - discovers only at the landing that none of it may land until all of it is committed. The repo's own answer is a sibling worktree per unit of work, and that answer is right; the point here is that the precondition makes the failure appear at the worst moment rather than at the start.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/loop.py`
- `src/basicly/merge.py`
- `tests/test_loop.py`

payload.value:
Given uncommitted changes in the base checkout that do not intersect the incoming merge then the advance proceeds and its detail names the dirt it admitted
Given uncommitted changes that do intersect the incoming merge then the advance refuses and names the intersecting paths
Given uncommitted engine tracker paths then the advance handles them as it does today, because it commits them itself
Given dirt a rebase would regenerate then it is admitted, on the same rule the landing already applies to a generated conflict
Demonstrated by: uv run pytest tests/test_loop.py -k dirt -q

payload.description:
## Context

The citation ratchet reports a stale `file:line` only when the cited line happens to be **blank or past end of file**. A citation that has drifted onto a different line of real code passes, and stays passing.

Measured 2026-08-17 on one block, `docs/plan/implementation-plan.md` around line 124, which tabulates three call sites:

| Cited | Actually at | Off by | Gate said |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `loop.py:869` `_run_agent` | 858 | 11 | passed |
| `loop.py:1119` `_run_proposer` | 1108 | 14 | **stale**, but only after an unrelated edit shifted it onto a blank line |
| `supervise.py:2651` `_dispatch_lane` | 2651 | 0 | passed, correctly |

Two of the three were wrong. The block was written 2026-08-15 in f8f6d34, so both survived two days and an unknown number of gate runs. The one the gate caught, it caught by luck: a three-line comment added elsewhere in `loop.py` pushed line 1119 onto a blank line.

## Why this is the worse failure mode

A citation pointing at nothing is an obvious defect. A citation pointing at the **wrong but existing** line reads as verified and is not — the same class the architecture rewrite hit, where three section references pointed at a real but wrong section. A reader who follows one lands on unrelated code and has no signal that the pointer, rather than their understanding, is what is wrong.

## What would fix it

The convention already exists and this repository states it: name the symbol, not the line. A symbol citation is checkable by search and survives every edit above it. The three entries above already name their symbol in the next column, which is why dropping the numbers cost nothing — that is the repair applied to the two stale ones in 1f3162b.

So the gate's own rule can be stronger: a `file:line` citation in a document is refusable on sight when the same entry names a symbol, and checkable against the symbol's definition line when it does not. What it must not do is treat a line's non-blankness as evidence.

## Scope

- `.scripts/check_docs_citations.py`
- `tests/test_check_docs_citations.py`
payload.title: the citation gate passes a line reference that drifted onto real code

payload.name: acceptance_criteria
payload.value:
Given a document citation naming both a symbol and a line then the gate refuses the line reference, because the symbol is the checkable half
Given a citation naming only a line and that line no longer holds the cited construct then the gate reports it stale, whether or not the line is blank
Given the two citations corrected in 1f3162b then a test pins that the gate would have refused them
Demonstrated by: uv run pytest tests/test_check_docs_citations.py -q

- `.scripts/check_docs_citations.py`
- `tests/test_check_docs_citations.py`

payload.name: description
payload.value:
Nothing spawns the external binary any more, and its vocabulary has not left. `basicly tracker write -- <argv>` takes the binary own argument grammar - comments add, close --reason, dep add, update --acceptance-criteria - and the seam translates it into owned events.

So every human tracker write, every skill that documents one, and every agent instruction still teaches a command language named after a tool the repository no longer runs. That is the same defect shape as the overloaded comment event kind, one layer up: a name inherited from a dependency outliving the dependency.

The choice is a design decision rather than a port. Either the seam grows a vocabulary of its own and the old grammar becomes an alias with a deprecation window, or the argv form is declared the permanent interface and the naming is accepted. Both are defensible; leaving it undecided means the next reader cannot tell which.

Filed from a retro rather than from a failure: no defect is attributable to it yet.

This record was minted by a probe of the create output path and repurposed rather than tombstoned.

## Context

`docs/research/2026-08-17-deepseek-harness.md` is findings, not a plan, and says so. A whole-tracker search for `sota|deepseek|cordis|revertible` over all 951 records returns one unrelated hit, so **nothing carries this work** — it exists only as research prose and as point 6 of the owner plan.

Two framing corrections the research establishes, both of which a proposal must respect. The paper formalises **Cordis**, not the harness; `deepseek` occurs once in it, as an author affiliation. And `dsh` is a **runtime, not a factory**: zero hits for `decompos`, `depends_on` and `blocked_by` across its packages, five for `worktree`, three for `git commit`, against a control of 3385 for `subagent`. It has no work graph, no decomposition and no landing, so it cannot teach us the loop. What it can teach us is composition, effect tracking and gated documentation.

## What must be settled before any adoption argument

Section 8 of the research lists eight open questions, each with a stated method. Two of them decide whether adoption is even possible, and they are this record.

**Q1 — does the revertible-effect guarantee survive contact with a filesystem?** The paper confines it to locations the system can modify exclusively and restore. A coding agent principal effects, files in a user repository, spawned processes and network calls, are outside that boundary by the paper own test. Method: enumerate `ctx.effect` call sites in the fs, shell and subprocess packages and classify each inverse as restore, compensate or no-op.

**Q4 — would the paradigm survive translation to Python?** The paper names the descriptor protocol as the `Proxy` analogue and requires a module registry supporting eviction. Neither claim is tested against CPython import machinery. Method: a spike that introduces a Python component and then **retracts** it, such that its registrations and its module both go away.

A proposal written before Q1 and Q4 are settled is unfalsifiable, which is why this record produces the answers first and the proposals second.

## Acceptance Criteria

Given Q1 then every `ctx.effect` call site in the three named packages is classified, with a count per class and the file and line for each.
Given Q4 then a runnable Python spike exists that introduces and retracts a component, and the transcript states which half failed if either did.
Given each settled question then a proposal names what basicly adopts, what it refuses, and the evidence for each, with a refusal reason stronger than taste.
Given a proposal that would change an invariant then it cites the invariant by architecture section number.
Given a question that could not be settled then it is listed as not established rather than answered from recall.
Demonstrated by: the spike script run end to end with its output pasted into the record, and a proposal set each item of which carries an evidence rung

## Scope

- `docs/research/`
- the tracker only. **This record writes no architecture text**; the architecture update is a separate record so the two do not collide.

payload.description:
## Context

Research 2026-08-19 established the routes and refuted the aggregator. `docs/research/` will carry the findings; this record builds the two halves.

**Half A, the route table.** `interface-facts` states a six rung order of evidence and its How to fetch section says to scope a search to the vendor and fetch the page. It names **no route**, so rung 3 costs an open ended search while recall costs nothing. Measured coverage of this repository own dependency set, all fetched 2026-08-19: six of ten vendors serve a first party `llms.txt` and per page markdown - uv, ruff, Claude Code, the Anthropic API, Codex and GitHub Docs. Python and pytest serve Sphinx `_sources/*.rst.txt` and an `objects.inv`. git and pre-commit serve neither and are answered at rung 2 by the installed binary. GitHub Docs publishes an Article and Search API explicitly for automated tools, with an **undocumented required parameter**: without `client_name` it answers 400 and names the missing parameter.

**Half B, the gate.** Nothing refuses a repository document that asserts a third party interface behaviour with no source, no version and no date. Four recurring memory entries are the same shape, and `check_docs_citations.py` is the precedent for a per document frozen ratchet.

## The rule the route table must not break

The instrument must stay **subordinate to rung 2**. Measured on this machine: `uv` installed 0.11.28 against 0.12.5 released, and `git` installed 2.43.0 against 2.55.0. `uv init` gained a default build system in 0.12.0, so the current documentation describes behaviour the installed binary does not have, and `uv init --help` on 0.11.28 already lists both `--package` and `--no-package`, so a flag probe misses it and only running the command finds the default. An instrument that makes fetching cheaper than running the binary therefore produces confidently wrong answers here.

## What it must refuse

Never be consulted before the installed binary. Never cache or commit fetched documentation, because a cache lands in a consumer tree and the licence exposure is real. Never cite an aggregator as the source of an interface fact. Never record a fact without its version and date.

## Not a new skill and not a tool skill

The `tool-*` family documents an installed binary and nothing here is installed, so that premise fails. This extends `interface-facts`, which already owns the doctrine. It is **not** a fragment: the always on baseline is measured at 7014 to 7343 characters and the tightest family cap is 974 away.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given a dependency this repository declares when a reader consults the skill then it names the machine readable route for that dependency or says the route is rung 2.
- Given the GitHub Docs route when it is documented then the required client name parameter is stated, because omitting it answers 400.
- Given the skill when a reader reaches the route table then the table sits below the instruction to run the installed binary first.
- Given a repository document asserting a third party interface behaviour with no adjacent source and version and date when the gate runs then it fails and names the document and the claim.
- Given an existing document already carrying such a claim then the gate holds it at a frozen per document count rather than failing the tree on day one.
- Given a route that has rotted then the gate does not silently pass, and the skill states that a route table needs a probe rather than trust.
- Demonstrated by: uv run basicly skills-check --all-default-roots and uv run basicly verify --mode full, plus the new gate failing on a deliberately unpinned claim and passing once the source and version and date are added

## Scope

- `.basicly/core/skills/interface-facts/`
- `.scripts/`
- `pyproject.toml`
- `tests/`
- `docs/research/`

(1) Ordering constraint that decides everything else: `basicly release` reads the changelog from the tagged commit, so a fragment edited after the tag never publishes. (2) If the owner ships as-is: the shipped CHANGELOG entry cannot be amended, so file a follow-up record under the existing dependent basicly-e2mz.48.2 ("refuse a document that asserts a third party interface behaviour with no source and version and date") to (a) restate the `client_name` line as a dated, network-conditional observation in skill.yaml, (b) fix "twelve rows"→eleven and "three of the twelve"→two, (c) name pyproject-fmt and pytest-xdist in the catch-all row, and ship the correction as a `fixed` fragment in the next release. (3) Standing gap to record, not to fix in this release: no gate in this repo probes a live third-party endpoint, and `docs-claims` catches only an invented command — every route row and the `client_name` sentence are unbindable by CI and will rot silently. The skill's own "probe the row before you quote it" is the only control, and it binds the reader, not the tree. COVERAGE BOUNDARY — what I did NOT inspect: the full pytest suite (I ran no `uv run pytest`); the .agents/ projection body (assumed identical to .claude/, covered only by the skills-check gate, not read); the historical uv 0.11.28-vs-0.12.5 incident underpinning the binary-first rationale (the toolchain has since been updated to 0.12.5, so it is now unverifiable from this machine); the ruff, platform.claude.com, per-page markdown, objects.inv and `_sources/*.rst.txt` routes, the 32 MB llms-full.txt figure, and the jinja2/rich probes; the `<redacted:posix-absolute-path>` and `<redacted:posix-absolute-path>` 200-without-client_name sub-claim (my guessed URL form returned 302, which tests my URL, not their claim). payload.description:
## Context

Nothing refuses a repository document that asserts a third party interface behaviour with no source, no version and no date. Four recurring memory entries are the same shape, and the cost is asymmetric: a wrong fact about our own code fails a gate, a wrong fact about someone elses interface is committed as prose and believed for months.

`.scripts/check_docs_citations.py` is the precedent. It walks documents for a `file:line` citation into code and holds each document at a frozen count, so an existing population does not fail the tree on day one while a new claim does.

## What the gate reads

A claim about an external interface, adjacent to a source URL, a version and a date it was verified at. The skill `interface-facts` already states the pinning rule and its own examples carry versions without dates, so the gate has a live population to bind on.

## What it must not do

It must not attempt to check that a fetched URL was the vendors. No gate can, and one that tried would fail open. Route correctness stays documentation tier; only the presence of source, version and date is mechanical.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given a document asserting a third party interface behaviour with no adjacent source and version and date when the gate runs then it fails and names the document and the claim.
- Given a document already carrying such a claim when the gate first runs then it holds that document at a frozen count rather than failing the tree.
- Given a frozen document whose count falls when the gate runs then the entry is reported as graduated rather than left stale.
- Given a claim that carries all three parts when the gate runs then it passes.
- Given the gate is added when the verify pipeline runs then it appears as a named check and the whole pipeline is green.

## Scope

- `.scripts/`
- `pyproject.toml`
- `basicly.toml`
- `tests/`

payload.description:
## Context

This is **P5-A**, the one adoption the DeepSeek review recommended out of five proposals. Section 11.3 of `docs/research/2026-08-17-deepseek-harness.md` carries the argument; P1 through P4 are refused there and must not be re-opened.

The harness wires two scripts into its gate runner that require a `## Model Experience` section per package with three named subsections, one of which is `Token effect`. The cost objection dies on measurement: `Model Experience` occurs **0** times across that project TypeScript against a positive control of 492 for `systemPrompt`, so the discipline costs zero model tokens. It is author facing, and it forces an author to state a cost they would otherwise not compute. That also answers open question 7 of the earlier research.

## Why this repository needs it, measured

The always on baseline sits at 7014 to 7343 characters and the tightest family cap is 974 characters away. A scoped fragment costs about 1500 characters of the always on file for one family and nothing for the other two. Nothing today makes an author state that before adding an entry, and the ratchet that would eventually refuse the last straw cannot attribute the cost to the author who never computed it.

## The carrier is refused even though the content is adopted

A per package markdown section would violate the rule that every catalog source is YAML and never markdown. So the requirement lands as a field on the YAML source and `basicly catalog lint` enforces it.

## The population and the risk, stated up front

**102 catalog YAML sources** carry no such field today: 41 skills, 21 fragments, 15 agents and the remainder targets, schemas and hooks. Every one gains a field, so the diff is large and mechanical. Splitting it by source family would be a horizontal cut with no consumer visible half, so it lands as one change and the size is reported rather than hidden.

The catalog schema is a **published contract** other repositories author against, so a newly required field needs a deprecation window rather than an immediate refusal.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given a catalog source with no declared token cost when the catalog lint runs in its warning window then it reports the source and does not fail.
- Given the warning window has passed when the catalog lint runs then a source with no declared token cost fails and names it.
- Given a declared token cost that disagrees with the measured projection by more than a stated tolerance when the lint runs then it reports the disagreement, so the field cannot rot.
- Given a source family that projects to nothing for a target when its cost is declared then the declaration states the per target cost rather than one number.
- Given the field is added to every source when the projection runs then the projected output is byte identical to before, because the field is authoring metadata and not content.
- Given the gate is added when the verify pipeline runs then it appears as a named check and the pipeline is green.

## Scope

- `.basicly/core/schemas/skill.schema.json`
- `.basicly/core/schemas/fragment.schema.json`
- `src/basicly/catalog_lint.py`
- `tests/test_catalog_lint.py`

[measured 2026-08-20, and it narrows this record rather than widening it]

Research section 11.3 adopts P5 as two halves. One half is a declared token cost on a catalog source, which is this record. The other half is the sharper import, stated as: every exemption list in basicly is machine validated against the population it exempts from, taken from the harness verify-package-readme-limitations.ts which fails an entry naming a package that no longer exists.

THE SECOND HALF IS ALREADY DISCHARGED. Measured across every exemption list in the tree, by reading each gate's comparison rather than its docstring:

- wired_or_deleted.BASELINE validates. Line 657 computes stale as BASELINE minus the reproducing findings and line 674 fails with `is in BASELINE but no longer reproduces`.
- check_module_size frozen entries validate, at lines 245 and 248, through ratchet.stale, with two distinct reasons: a waiver replaces the frozen entry, and no readable tracked module is at this path.
- check_comment_density frozen entries validate, at lines 225 and 228, the same way.
- recall_eval.FAMILY_BASELINE validates, at lines 141 to 145, failing when a baseline rule has no anchors and would score zero for free.
- check_noqa_debt validates, by a DIFFERENT mechanism, and this is the one that needs recording because the obvious probe reports it as missing. It does not import ratchet.stale, so a search for stale callers returns four hits and misses it. It iterates the UNION at line 285, `for code in sorted(set(counts) | set(ratchet.frozen))`, so a frozen code with zero occurrences is still visited and fires _fell at line 231 with `the record still licenses N`. Same effect, no stale call.

Probe discipline for whoever re-checks this: searching for ratchet.stale callers is the wrong probe and it under reports by one of five. The right probe is whether the gate's comparison visits the frozen set independently of the observed set. My own first reading of check_noqa_debt was wrong for exactly this reason, and the union at line 285 is what corrected it.

Note dropin.compose_ratchet line 133, `kept = {key: value for key, value in composed.items() if value != 0}`, drops a composed zero from the baseline rather than reporting it. That is not a hole here, because each gate visits its own frozen set, but it means a fragment can retire an entry silently and no gate names the retirement.

SO THIS RECORD SHOULD NOT CLAIM THE EXEMPTION VALIDATION RULE AS NEW. Its scope is the declared token cost only, in YAML because section 10.2 requires every catalog source to be YAML, enforced by basicly catalog lint, as section 36.7's fifth gate kind, a catalog source assertion on declared token cost. A release note claiming basicly gained machine validated exemption lists would be false: it had five of five before this record starts.

RELATED, and possibly the real remaining defect in this area: basicly-oa9f says the suppression lists cite the wrong file and carry a stale count. That is a stale citation and a stale number inside lists that DO self validate, which is a different failure from an unvalidated list. Check whether oa9f is the actual residue of P5's second half before filing anything new.

payload.description:
## The defect

`.scripts/check_docs_citations.py` walks `docs/**/*.md` for a file and line reference into code, and reports 33 citations in 17 documents with 0 stale. **Nothing runs the other direction.** A section reference written in code, pointing at a document, is unchecked, so it goes stale in silence. A citation that resolves to the **wrong** section is worse than no citation, because it reads as correct.

This is `docs/architecture/backlog.md` entry B2, which has sat in an ungated second backlog rather than in the tracker. Its own cost estimate is 25 edits. That estimate counts one population of four.

## Measured 2026-08-19, four populations

| Population | Count |
| --- | --- |
| Citations naming the architecture explicitly | 25 |
| Citations naming factory-loop.md explicitly | 10 |
| Citations naming work-tracker.md explicitly | 1 |
| Bare section references inside the tracker kit, which the module headers bind to work-tracker.md | **127** |
| Bare section references elsewhere in the tree | 233 |

So 36 named and 360 bare. The bare ones are the problem the direction check exists for: a reader cannot tell which document a bare reference means, and neither can a gate.

The kit case is the sharpest. The kit is a standalone consumable. Each module names its source document once in the header and then uses bare references, so a consumer who installs the kit alone receives 127 pointers into a document that was never shipped to them. That is live today, before any deletion.

## Why this must land before the absorption

`basicly-1hp91f` deletes factory-loop.md and `basicly-vkh0.42.13` deletes work-tracker.md. Both would orphan their citations with every gate green, because the direction that would catch it does not exist. The check is the control; the absorptions are the changes that need it.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Run the documentation citation checker and observe it reports citations found in documents, pointing at code.
2. Search the tree for a section reference written in code and observe hundreds.
3. Pick one bare reference in a kit module and try to determine which document it means from the line alone. Observe you cannot without reading the module header.
4. Delete a heading the architecture defines and re-run every gate. Observe all green.

Observed: a code to document citation cannot be validated by any gate, and a bare reference cannot even be attributed to a document.
Expected: a section reference from code resolves to a heading that exists, and a bare reference is either attributed or refused.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given a section reference in code that names a document when the check runs then it resolves to a heading that document currently defines, or the check fails naming the file and line and the missing number.
- Given a bare section reference when the check runs then it is attributed to a document by a declared per module or per directory binding, or it is reported as unattributable.
- Given every citation resolving when the check runs then it exits zero and prints the citation count.
- Given a deleted heading when the check runs then it fails with exactly one failure naming the citing site.
- Given the existing population when the check first runs then it is frozen per file, so the backlog does not block a commit while a new stale citation does.
- Given the check is added when the verify pipeline runs then it appears as a named check and the pipeline is green.

## Scope

- `.scripts/check_docs_citations.py`
- `pyproject.toml`
- `basicly.toml`
- `tests/test_docs_citations.py`

payload.description:
## Context

Owner decision 2026-08-14, settling the question `factory-loop.md` section 6.3 has carried open since
2026-08-08 under the heading *"Unresolved, and section 6.2 requires it resolved"*. The question was
carried by no bead at all, which is why it survived three sessions.

`code-reviewer` and `reviewer` differ in invoker and artifact but not in job. Section 6.2 requires
that overlap resolved rather than left as two things with one job, and D5 admits a role only when it
differs in tier, tools or artifact.

**The owner supersedes `code-reviewer`.** `reviewer` is the stronger definition and section 6.3 says
why: per-lens, adversarial stance, severity-bounded, and no cross-lens ranking. `basicly-feje` made
it reachable on 2026-08-14, dispatched once per lens at VALIDATE, and `basicly-w88t` made its
findings reach a repair. It is a live role with a contract; `code-reviewer` is a prompt.

## This is a breaking change to a shipped surface, and that is the whole difficulty

`code-reviewer` is projected into every agent root and **vendored to consumers by `basicly install`**.
Removing it deletes an agent a consumer may invoke by name today. Section 6.3 records exactly this as
the reason the decision was the owner's rather than the document's.

So it is not a delete. Three things have to happen together, and the order matters.

- The commit carries a `!` marker and a `BREAKING CHANGE:` footer naming the removed agent and its
  replacement. The `v0.6.0` audit exists because zero of 535 commits carried a marker, and plan
  section 7 makes the marker a gate after the freeze.
- A deprecation window ships before the removal, not with it. A consumer who invokes
  `code-reviewer` gets told what replaced it, on the surface they used, rather than getting nothing.
- `reviewer` must be invocable the way `code-reviewer` was. Today it is engine-invoked at VALIDATE
  only. A human who typed `code-reviewer` needs a route, or the supersession removes a capability
  instead of relocating one.

That third point is the one that can turn this into a regression, and it is where the work is.

## What must not be taken from the removal

The two lenses are `correctness` and `security`, chosen deliberately in section 6.5 because a lens
whose axis a gate already covers spends tokens to restate a green check. Maintainability was refused
because ruff, pyright, vulture, `lint-imports`, `module-size`, `comment-density` and `noqa-debt`
ratchet it mechanically. Do not widen the lens vocabulary to cover what `code-reviewer` used to say.

## Acceptance

- When the catalog is built, then `code-reviewer` is absent from every projected agent root and from
  the vendored set, and `reviewer` is present in both.
- While a consumer invokes the superseded name, when the harness resolves it, then it reports the
  replacement rather than failing silently or resolving to nothing.
- When a human wants an ad-hoc review, then a documented route to `reviewer` exists that does not
  require a VALIDATE dispatch.
- When the change lands, then the commit carries a breaking marker and a changelog fragment naming
  the removed agent.
- When the lens vocabulary is read after the change, then it is still exactly `correctness` and
  `security`.

## Scope

- `.basicly/core/agents/code-reviewer/`
- `.basicly/core/agents/reviewer/`
- `src/basicly/roles.py`
- `tests/test_roles.py`
- `tests/test_agents.py`
- `docs/requirements/factory-loop.md` section 6.3
- `changelog.d/`

## Demonstration

`uv run basicly agents-check --all-default-roots` passes with `code-reviewer` gone, a fresh
`basicly install` into a scratch repo writes `reviewer` and not `code-reviewer`, and invoking the old
name reports the replacement. Read that output rather than asserting it.

Gap 2 was already met and recorded (basicly-j73p); the one-lane bound re-observed against real tracker state.
